keyVerseText: Is any thing too hard for the LORD? At the time appointed I will return unto thee, according to the time of life, and Sarah shall have a son.
rootMeaning: The Hebrew verb פָּלָא (pâlâʼ) is a primitive root that conveys the idea of being extraordinary or surpassing ordinary limits. Its core sense involves separating or distinguishing something as remarkable or difficult, which goes beyond the common English gloss of 'marvelous' or 'wondrous.' This root sense highlights the notion of setting apart that which is beyond human capability or understanding, emphasizing the exceptional nature of what is accomplished or revealed.
usageInScripture: Across its 71 occurrences, pâlâʼ consistently describes actions or works that are extraordinary, difficult, or beyond human power to perform. It is translated variously as 'too hard,' 'marvellous things,' and 'wondrous things,' reflecting a semantic range that centers on the miraculous and the surpassing nature of God's deeds. This consistency reveals that the word is primarily used to express the divine ability to accomplish what is otherwise impossible or hidden, underscoring God's unique power and majesty.
theologicalSignificance: Theologically, pâlâʼ underscores the transcendence and omnipotence of God, highlighting that His works are beyond human comprehension and ability. This word reminds believers that God's actions are not merely extraordinary but are fundamentally set apart as miraculous and wondrous. Recognizing this enriches faith by affirming that God's power surpasses all natural limits, inviting trust in His sovereign will and providence. It also points to the divine initiative in salvation and revelation, where God performs what no one else can, thus glorifying Him as the source of all marvels.
keyVerseReflection: In Genesis 18:14, the question 'Is any thing too hard for the LORD?' uses pâlâʼ to emphasize that nothing is beyond God's power to accomplish. This verse reassures believers that God's promises, such as the birth of Isaac to Sarah, will be fulfilled despite natural impossibilities. The word pâlâʼ here highlights God's ability to perform wonders at the appointed time, reinforcing trust in His faithfulness and omnipotence.
